title: Mecka AI Nears $500M Valuation in Sequoia-Led Round for Robot Training Data
excerpt: The humanoid data startup would be valued at roughly five times its last round just three months ago, as investors race to own the physical-world datasets behind general-purpose robots.
body:
• Mecka AI, a startup that turns human motion into training data for humanoid robots, is nearing a new funding round led by Sequoia Capital at a valuation of about $500 million, TechCrunch reported on September 11, citing two people familiar with the deal.
  • The financing would come just three months after Mecka disclosed a $60 million raise led by Framework Ventures — a $25 million Series A closed in November and a $35 million follow-on investment.
  • Mecka pays people to record everyday tasks with body sensors and smartphones, and sells the datasets to robotics companies and AI labs. It was projecting a $100 million annual run rate by the end of 2026.
  • The round is not final and terms could still change; the size of the new financing has not been disclosed.

Mecka AI is nearing a new funding round led by Sequoia Capital at a valuation of about $500 million, according to two people with knowledge of the deal — a price that would value the human-motion data startup at roughly five times the level implied by its previous raise just three months earlier.

TechCrunch reported the talks on September 11, cautioning that the round's size is unknown and terms could still change. Mecka did not respond to a request for comment; Sequoia declined to comment.

Context & Background

Mecka, founded in 2024 and based in New York City, was started by four entrepreneurs from fintech and crypto rather than robotics: Canadians Josh Gao and Mogen Cheng, who previously built a restaurant fintech startup; Jason Chong, who joined Coinbase after it acquired his crypto exchange; and Duy Nguyen, the only non-Canadian on the team, who runs operations. The name comes from "mecha," the fictional giant robots controlled by humans.

The founders' insight was about the bottleneck. General-purpose robots are held back less by hardware than by a shortage of physical-world data: records of how real bodies move through messy, unpredictable environments. Mecka pays people to record themselves performing everyday tasks using body sensors and smartphones, then sells that "egocentric" motion data to robotics companies and AI labs training their models. CEO Gao told Fortune the company had already gathered thousands of gigabytes of such data and saw enough demand from signed contracts to reach a $100 million annual revenue run rate by the end of 2026, though he declined to name customers.

The previous financing surfaced in early June as two undisclosed rounds: a $25 million Series A closed in November and a $35 million follow-on investment, totaling $60 million. Framework Ventures led both, with Menlo Ventures, SV Angel, Kindred Ventures, and former Google DeepMind researcher Ted Xiao participating. Framework co-founder Vance Spencer told Fortune that Mecka was the fastest-growing company his firm had backed — proof, he said, that the market for robot training data is real.

"Mecka is the fastest-growing company his firm has backed, calling the business proof that the market is real."

— Vance Spencer, co-founder, Framework Ventures (via Fortune)

Impact & Analysis

Mecka is attempting to do for robotics what Scale AI, Mercor, and Surge did for large language models: build the human-data layer underneath an entire industry. Physical AI needs a supply chain for capturing how humans move, grasp, and manipulate objects — the way LLMs needed one for labeling and refining the internet's text.

The thesis is drawing heavy money on multiple fronts. TechCrunch reported last week that XDOF, another startup collecting real-world data for robot training, was nearing a new round at a $1.2 billion valuation — more than double Mecka's prospective price — while LLM-era data platforms like Scale AI and Micro1 are expanding into physical AI too. Mecka's bet is that the data layer is the scarcest of the three — robot makers, model builders, data suppliers — letting it sell into many robotics programs rather than gambling on a single hardware platform.

That a crypto-native firm like Framework led Mecka's last round and Sequoia is now circling shows how fast the narrative has shifted — toward data, not hardware, as the scarce layer in robotics.

Diaspora Angle

The deal lands in a sector where Indian-origin engineers and researchers are already deeply embedded — at AI labs, robotics companies, and data platforms expanding into physical AI.

What's Next

The Sequoia-led round is not finalized, so the first thing to watch is whether it closes at the reported $500 million figure — and at what size. The second is whether Mecka can sustain the growth it is projecting, as turning thousands of gigabytes of collected data into a $100 million run rate will test whether the egocentric-data model can scale as fast as investors are pricing in. With XDOF, Scale AI, and Micro1 chasing the same thesis, the race to own the physical-data layer is fully on.
